verdict: OK to lend in Moradabad non-ferrous and brass fabrication, but only to exporters and organised fabricators with metal-price pass-through and hedged working capital; avoid artisan-dependent job-work units and unhedged single-buyer exporters.
title: Moradabad Non-ferrous Metals, Brass & Fabricated Metal: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
Moradabad melts and fabricates non-ferrous metal into brassware, artware and industrial castings, then sells largely into export markets; the city's brass trade is put at ₹11,460 crore of exports [2]. **Cash is made on conversion margin, not on metal** — the metal is a pass-through input, so the borrower's real economics sit in yield, scrap recovery and finishing labour. The binding constraint is skilled labour: local reporting says the traditional craft is under stress and preparing the next generation of artisans is a challenge [1]. So when a proposal lands, check how much of the process is in-house versus outsourced to artisan job-work; if the unit depends on a handful of karigars, ask what happens to delivery if that bench thins.

## Where value and cash sit
**Working capital is the loan, not the machine.** Metal inventory plus export receivables dominate the balance sheet, and rating experience in this space shows moderately high working-capital requirements supported by bank lines [10], with fund-based limit utilisation running as high as 88% at a comparable metal borrower [9]. Pricing power is thin against global buyers, so margin comes from buying scrap and alloy well and turning stock fast. Capex is modest — furnaces, polishing and plating — and rating commentary treats modest capex as normal for such units [9]. So when a proposal lands, check stock turns and receivable days against limit utilisation; if drawing power is pegged near the limit for months, ask for the ageing of export receivables and the scrap-to-finished yield.

## What has changed now
**The demand signal is strong but the local craft base is the weak link.** India-wide output for NIC 25 is up 16.9% YoY and 12.0% Apr-to-date [D], and UP GST collections are running 14.2% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1% [D]. Bank credit is growing 11.9% against output of 12.0%, a gap of -0.1 pp [D] — funding is broadly keeping pace, not overheating. Peer results confirm volume-led growth: Gravita's Q2 FY27 revenue rose 38% with volumes of 52,199 MT up 3% [4][6], and KSH International's Q3 FY26 revenue rose 59% on volumes up 24% [5]. Against that, the local artisan shortage [1] and the push to link brass trade to e-commerce and global markets [2][3] mean the winners will be units that can scale without depending on inherited hand skills. Note the peer results are national, not Moradabad-specific; local sources say little on city-level credit data, so lean on first principles here.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue organised fabricators and exporters with diversified buyer books, in-house finishing and documented metal hedging; avoid pure job-work units and single-buyer exporters.** Structure term debt short — three to five years — and keep working capital as the core exposure, with a cash-flow cycle that matches the export receivable tenor. Take monthly stock and receivable statements, quarterly GST returns reconciled to sales, and a metal-price hedging confirmation each quarter. Where the borrower sells only to one overseas buyer, ask for the buyer contract and payment history before sanctioning.

## Early-warning signs
- **Limit utilisation above 88% for two straight months [9] -> freeze enhancements and re-cut drawing power.**
- **Receivable days stretching while volumes hold -> ask for buyer-wise ageing and confirm the export buyer is paying.**
- **Artisan attrition or delivery delays reported locally [1] -> re-assess execution risk and tighten stock norms.**
- **Scrap availability or price swings compressing yield -> ask for the monthly yield report and hedge cover.**
watch: Utilisation above 88% for two months -> freeze enhancements, re-cut drawing power
GST sales falling below bank-statement turnover -> ask for reconciliation and stop fresh disbursal
Unhedged metal exposure above borrower's stated policy -> require hedge before next renewal
Top buyer above half of sales or receivables past due -> seek buyer contract and payment proof
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
news_why: Local artisan shortage threatens execution even as national output and UP GST run strong.
